name: Cyclops Vigil
geological_features: A single massive crater dominating one hemisphere, giving the body a concave profile
Exposed metallic core visible at the crater floor
Regolith of pulverized rock and metal fragments
specific_features: The crater focus point reflects sunlight in a concentrated beam visible from neighboring worlds
resources: Exposed core metals including iron, nickel, and cobalt
description: Cyclops Vigil is a world with one eye. A cataclysmic impact in its distant past carved a crater so large it dominates an entire hemisphere, scooping out crust and mantle to expose the metallic core beneath. The result is a body with a concave face that catches and focuses sunlight into a brilliant reflected beam, a natural lighthouse visible across the system that has served as a navigational reference since the first ships entered these coordinates.

The crater interior is a bowl of exposed metal and fractured rock, its walls terraced by the impact's shockwaves into concentric rings that descend to the gleaming core floor. The thin atmosphere pools in the crater depression, marginally thicker and warmer than the barren exterior. Walking the crater rim, one looks down into a metallic basin that curves to the horizon in all directions, its reflective surface creating a disorienting sense of standing on the lip of a mirror.

The focused reflection was initially mistaken for an artificial signal by early system probes, leading to a first-contact protocol that was stood down only after physical survey confirmed the phenomenon was natural. The crater geometry that produces the focusing effect is remarkably precise, a coincidence that some researchers find difficult to accept. The impact that created it should have shattered a body this small entirely, and models of the event require specific conditions so narrow that the probability borders on the absurd.

Cyclops Vigil's exposed core metals are commercially significant and unusually accessible, requiring no subsurface mining. Several firms have established automated extraction operations on the crater floor, using the reflection beam's predictable geometry to site their solar collectors. The body's position and its beacon-like visibility make it a natural system hub, and a small station on the crater rim serves as a waypoint for traffic through the region. The question of whether the crater is truly natural persists in academic circles but affects operations not at all.
